skills.title: Indigenous Nations Before 1713
skills.description: Many Indigenous nations met Europeans long ago, like the Wendat, Mi'kmaq, Cree, and Inuit. Match each nation to where it lived and how it lived.

skills.title: Nations Trading and Allying
skills.description: Before Europeans came, First Nations and Inuit traded, made alliances, and sometimes competed for waterways. Pick which one each story shows.

skills.title: Why Europeans Came
skills.description: Explorers and settlers came for fur, fish, land, and to spread their religion. Match people like Cabot, Cartier, and Champlain to why they came.

skills.title: Who Mattered in New France
skills.description: New France had a king, governor, bishop, intendant, seigneurs, and priests and nuns. Match each one to what it did for settlers.

skills.title: Indigenous and European Meetings
skills.description: When Indigenous peoples and Europeans met, they traded, shared skills, fought, and spread disease. Match each event to what happened.

skills.title: How the Métis People Began
skills.description: The Métis nation began when fur traders and First Nations women married and built families. Pick the reasons it began in the Great Lakes and Mattawa areas.

skills.title: How Ways of Life Differed
skills.description: Indigenous and European communities had different ways of governing, using land, and living. Match each difference to its reason, like climate or old customs.

skills.title: European Fights Reach Canada
skills.description: Wars between France and Britain pulled in First Nations and changed who controlled places like Acadia. Match each conflict to its effect.

skills.title: Good and Bad Results of Contact
skills.description: Contact brought alliances and new ideas, but also disease, lost land, and conflict. Sort each result into positive or negative.

skills.title: Who Gained From Whom
skills.description: Europeans gained from Indigenous knowledge of land, medicines, and routes. First Nations gained new tools. Match each group to what it gained.

skills.title: Past Contact and Canada Today
skills.description: Old treaties and land use still link to land claims and treaty rights today. Match each past event to the issue it connects to now.

skills.title: Questions About Early Contact
skills.description: Pick a good question about how a group, like coureurs de bois or First Nations women, saw early contact.

skills.title: Sources With Different Views
skills.description: Treaties, journals, petroglyphs, and oral histories are sources. Sort which ones give which group's view.

skills.title: Maps of Contact and Trade
skills.description: Read maps of trade routes, First Nations territory, and Métis communities. Pick what each map shows.

skills.title: Checking Evidence and Comparing Views
skills.description: Pick whether evidence is accurate and has an authentic voice. Use a comparison chart to compare views on the fur trade.

skills.title: Conclusions About Early Contact
skills.description: Look at the evidence and pick the conclusion it supports about how different groups saw contact.

skills.title: Sharing Early Contact Findings
skills.description: Pick the best way to share what you learned, and words like treaty, missionary, settler, and wampum belt.

skills.title: Rights and Responsibilities in Canada
skills.description: Citizens have rights like voting and free speech, and duties like respecting others. Sort each into a right or a responsibility.

skills.title: Levels of Government and Services
skills.description: Federal, provincial, municipal, band councils, and school boards each run different services. Match each service, like police or garbage pickup, to who provides it.

skills.title: First Nations, Métis, Inuit Governments
skills.description: Groups like the Métis Nation of Ontario and the Haudenosaunee Confederacy govern today. Match each to who it represents.

skills.title: Governments Sharing the Work
skills.description: Some jobs, like health care and the environment, are shared by several levels of government. Match each to the levels that share it.

skills.title: How Governments Ask the Public
skills.description: Elections, town halls, and referendums let people share their views. Match each way to how it works, and pick why asking people matters.

skills.title: The Duty to Consult
skills.description: Governments must talk with and make room for Indigenous communities about things like pipelines or mines on their land. Pick when this duty applies.

skills.title: What Governments Do About Issues
skills.description: Governments make recycling programs, laws, and language projects to solve problems. Match each action to the issue it helps with.

skills.title: Why Views on Issues Differ
skills.description: Farmers, companies, governments, and Indigenous groups may see an issue differently. Match each group to why it feels that way.

skills.title: How Citizens Take Action
skills.description: People can sign petitions, vote, volunteer, or write to leaders. Pick the best action for each problem.

skills.title: Did the Government Action Work?
skills.description: Look at what a government did about an issue and pick whether it worked well and why.

skills.title: Plan for a Social Issue
skills.description: Put the steps of a plan about an issue like homelessness in order, and pick what governments and citizens should each do.

skills.title: Plan for an Environmental Issue
skills.description: Put the steps of a plan about an issue like waste or clean water in order, and pick what governments and citizens should each do.

skills.title: Questions About Canadian Issues
skills.description: Pick a good question to investigate an issue, like climate change in the Arctic, from the view of a government or Indigenous group.

skills.title: Gathering Facts on Issues
skills.description: Sort sources, like Elder interviews, graphs, and government statements, by the view they show about an issue.

skills.title: Maps of Issues
skills.description: Read maps that show things like areas hit by climate change or poverty across provinces. Pick what each map shows.

skills.title: Graphs and Idea Webs on Issues
skills.description: Read line graphs, double bar graphs, and idea webs about an issue like recycling. Pick what they show.

skills.title: Conclusions About Issues
skills.description: Use the evidence to pick a conclusion about an issue, and pick the strengths and weaknesses of different views.

skills.title: Sharing Issue Findings
skills.description: Pick the best way to share what you learned, and words like municipal, federal, MP, band council, and stakeholder.
